front: Give the thesis in one sentence.
back: A computational method that takes Barcelona's tree-plan rules as constraints and chooses which species replace Porta's plane trees and where, scoring each layout on pedestrian heat stress (UTCI) and event runoff volume, and showing the trade-off (Pareto front).

front: Why will Barcelona replace many plane trees?
back: The tree master plan caps any species at 15%, and plane trees are 27.45% of the city's trees (press 2026); the city will cut them by 56% to 12% in ten years.

front: How much did Barcelona's sealed surface grow, and when?
back: From 45% to 72% of the municipality, 1956–2009.

front: How often do intense storms hit Barcelona?
back: About 3 storms a year exceed 60 mm/h in their first 20 minutes (Barcelona Resilience Atlas).

front: What heat-health fact frames Barcelona's heat problem?
back: It carries one of Europe's highest urban-heat-island mortality burdens (Iungman et al. 2023).

front: Name the seven palette species, and say which two the city does not name as plane replacements.
back: Celtis australis, Melia azedarach, Pyrus calleryana, Jacaranda mimosifolia, Tipuana tipu, Brachychiton populneus, Styphnolobium japonicum. Not named by the city as plane replacements: Jacaranda and Brachychiton (v6).

front: Which replacement species has a measured canopy-storage value?
back: Only Pyrus calleryana (Xiao & McPherson 2016). For cooling, only Pyrus (surface temperature, abstract) and Tipuana (tropical field and modelled) have any value. Styphnolobium has measured event interception (Yang 2019), not a storage value.

front: Which flood type does the thesis address, and which does it exclude?
back: Urban pluvial flooding from frequent, short storms. It excludes river (fluvial) floods and multi-day events on saturated soil.

front: Why was Bologna dropped as a flood case?
back: Its recent floods (Oct 2024, May 2023 Emilia-Romagna) were multi-day, saturated-soil or culvert events where trees have negligible influence.

front: Who is the primary user of the tool?
back: A computational designer working on the municipal street-tree replacement.

front: What is the risk the problem statement points to?
back: Replacement choices can trade away cooling or rain interception without anyone noticing, because most replacement species have no measured storage or cooling value.

front: Where is the study site and how big is it?
back: Porta, Nou Barris, Barcelona; 0.84 km².

front: How many plane trees in Porta, and where are most?
back: 832 plane trees (29% of 2,825 street trees); 194 on Av. Meridiana.

front: What were the two steps of site selection?
back: 1) Eligibility: flood share, surface-heat anomaly and plane density all above the city's 60th percentile. 2) Ranking by the equal-weight mean of four normalised criteria.

front: What does 'non-compensatory' mean in the site selection?
back: A strong value on one hazard cannot make up for the absence of the other: every criterion must pass the threshold first.

front: How was the site choice tested for robustness?
back: Thresholds at the 50th, 60th and 70th percentiles: Porta is first at every threshold. 2,000 random (Dirichlet) weightings: Porta is in the top 3 in 53% of them.

front: Porta's ranks for flood, surface heat and heat vulnerability?
back: Flood #13, surface heat #11 (+1.36 °C), heat vulnerability #12 (91% of area in the top class).

front: What are the four site-selection criteria?
back: Pluvial flood hazard share, summer surface-temperature anomaly (Landsat), social heat vulnerability, plane-tree density.

front: Why is Sant Antoni not the main site?
back: It is #1 for flood but #38 for surface heat (below the city median), so it fails the both-hazards condition. It is the flood-dominant contrast site.

front: What is Florence's role?
back: Transfer test case: run the same method to see if trade-off pattern and species ranking hold.

front: Why does it help that the replacement palette already grows in Porta?
back: Real crowns, heights and LAI of each species can be measured on site from LiDAR.

front: Describe the runoff chain in the model.
back: Rain → canopy interception (storage bucket) over crowns on sealed ground → remaining rain → SCS curve number → event runoff volume.

front: Write the interception equation.
back: I = min(P, S), with S = s · LAI (P rain depth, S canopy storage in mm, s storage per unit LAI).

front: What is the calibrated value of s and its source?
back: s = 1.75 mm per unit LAI, calibrated on Anys & Weiler (2024) Freiburg field data: 16 urban lime and maple trees, 51 storms.

front: What is the lower bound of s in sensitivity runs, and why?
back: 0.86 mm: surface storage only, without evaporation during events (Xiao & McPherson 2016).

front: How much rain does a leafy crown hold at the start of a storm?
back: The first 2–4 mm (Kuehler et al. 2017).

front: Curve numbers used for sealed and pervious surfaces?
back: 98 for sealed surfaces and roofs; 74 for pervious (assumption: TR-55 open space, soil group C).

front: Design storm depths (60 min) for T = 1, 2, 10 years?
back: 19.6 mm, 31.9 mm, 62.5 mm (PDISBA city IDF).

front: Why is the metric runoff volume, not peak flow?
back: In a paired-catchment field study, street trees cut runoff volume ~4% with no peak-flow effect (Selbig et al. 2021).

front: What is the field benchmark for street-tree runoff reduction?
back: 3.5–4% of runoff volume (Coville et al. 2022; Selbig et al. 2021).

front: Why does the tree effect shrink as storms grow?
back: Canopy storage fills in the first few mm; the rest of a big storm passes through, so the intercepted share falls.

front: What is the main trait driving interception?
back: Leaf area index (LAI) / leaf area density; storage capacity also varies threefold among 20 species (Xiao & McPherson 2016).

front: Why are roots not in the scoring?
back: Only two lab studies (Bartens 2008; Zhang 2019): roots raise infiltration, but species differences are unclear (oak vs maple not significant).

front: Why is stemflow ignored?
back: It is < 1% of rain (Anys & Weiler 2024).

front: What is a return period T?
back: The average interval between storms of that size; T = 10 yr means about a 10% chance per year.

front: What sewer design level does Barcelona use?
back: A 10-year return period.

front: What is UTCI?
back: Universal Thermal Climate Index: the 'felt' temperature for a pedestrian, from air temperature, humidity, wind and mean radiant temperature.

front: Which UTCI input do trees change most?
back: Mean radiant temperature (MRT), through shade.

front: UTCI threshold for strong heat stress?
back: UTCI > 32 °C.

front: Write the canopy transmissivity formula.
back: τ = exp(−k · LAI), with k = 0.5 (Beer–Lambert).

front: What is Ladybug Tier 1?
back: Fast point-based UTCI at 1.1 m on a 2 m sidewalk grid, used for many layouts.

front: Two reasons Ladybug underestimates tree cooling.
back: Crowns are opaque without the τ correction (shade MRT off), and it has no evapotranspiration (~2–3 °C UTCI, Mannucci 2025).

front: What is Tier 2 in the heat module?
back: Honeybee UTCI comfort map (Radiance + EnergyPlus) with leaf-on/off transmittance, for a few final layouts.

front: What is Infrared City's role?
back: An AI surrogate API for UTCI in seconds (tutor co-founded it); would replace Tier 1 inside the optimiser. Access still to confirm.

front: Why does the optimiser need a heat proxy?
back: Ladybug costs minutes per layout (20–25 min for 42 trees, Shaamala 2025); 832 positions × many layouts is too slow.

front: Which is the stronger air-cooling term, shade or transpiration?
back: Transpiration (Park 2026: 1.15 °C vs shade 0.43 °C), but it needs soil water.

front: What happened to Platanus in an extreme heatwave?
back: It lost roughly 30–50% of its plant area index after > 41 °C (Sanusi & Livesley 2020) → low-LAI plane variant in sensitivity.

front: Which traits help both heat and runoff?
back: LAI and crown size.

front: Which traits create the heat–runoff conflict?
back: Leaf habit (evergreen vs deciduous) and transpiration / water demand.

front: Why did the leaf-on calendar not create a trade-off?
back: 78% of intense storm days fall in May–Oct (Esbrí et al. 2026), when all palette species are in full leaf.

front: What created the first real trade-off in tool v0?
back: Winter sun access: winter shade on sunlit open ground counted as a cost.

front: Mnemonic for the trade-off finding?
back: Big crowns win both; leaves in winter split them.

front: What is the gap in one sentence (safe wording)?
back: No method yet chooses street-tree species and positions against pedestrian-level UTCI and event runoff together.

front: What is SylvCiT and what is missing?
back: A trait-based AI tree recommender (Nicol et al. 2026, Montreal); its runoff module is disabled, it has no heat, and it uses diversity traits.

front: What does Mannucci et al. 2025 do, and lack?
back: Grasshopper + Ladybug + Kangaroo assess UTCI and runoff, but for fixed scenarios, with no species traits and no optimisation.

front: Which works optimise trees for heat only?
back: Shaamala et al. 2025 and Peng et al. 2026 (Shaamala names water sensitivity as future work).

front: What is the closest precedent?
back: Tan & Liu 2026: NSGA-II + Random Forest surrogate in Grasshopper, species and positions of 30 trees for UTCI, CO2 and diversity.

front: What does this thesis add to Tan & Liu 2026?
back: Runoff, the city's own replacement palette, and the seasons (leaf calendar, winter sun). They used 4 Chicago species, US allometry, one summer hour.

front: Why is the trait data gap itself a finding?
back: Most of the city's replacement species have no measured storage or cooling value; the method has to fill gaps with ranges, and the gap is reported.

front: State the research question (short form).
back: In Porta, which replacement species, chosen within the tree master plan's rules (15% cap, size class by sidewalk width, the city's catalogue), and at which plane positions, jointly reduce pedestrian heat stress (mean UTCI over 12-17 h on a hot design day) and event runoff volume (1-, 2-, 10-yr PDISBA storms), and how large is the trade-off against the current trees and the city's own replacement. (v6, 21 Oct: the rules and the city's replacement entered the RQ.)

front: What is H1?
back: Synergy: at the same positions and the size classes the sidewalks allow, trait-based choices beat the city's own replacement (S1) on both UTCI and runoff, because crown size and LAI drive both.

front: What is H2?
back: Trade-off: heat-optimal and runoff-optimal layouts differ mainly in species (leaf habit, transpiration), not positions; the Pareto front is not a single point.

front: What happened to H3?
back: Withdrawn on 19 Oct. It said the runoff benefit shrinks as the return period grows - true, but the bucket model cannot fail it (I = min(P, S), every crown full at every storm), so it is an identity, not a test. It is kept as a declared validity boundary of the method: small benefit at T = 10 yr, extreme events (6 Sept 2018, ~300-yr) outside what trees can affect.

front: Mnemonic for the hypotheses?
back: S-T: Synergy, Trade-off - the two that are tested. The old third letter, B for Boundary, is the withdrawn H3: still said out loud, but as a declared boundary of the method, not a hypothesis (19 Oct).

front: Which comparison tests each hypothesis?
back: H1: S4 vs S1 on both objectives. H2: species composition of S2 vs S3 at the same fixed positions. H3 is no longer tested - it was withdrawn on 19 Oct and is reported as a declared boundary.

front: List scenarios S0–S4.
back: S0 current trees; S1 the city's own replacement (2026 mix within the sizing rule); S2 heat-only optimum; S3 runoff-only optimum; S4 multi-objective Pareto set.

front: Mnemonic for S0–S4?
back: Now, Swap, Hot, Wet, Both.

front: Which optimiser is planned, and what does v0 use?
back: NSGA-II (pymoo or Wallacei); v0 uses a weighted-sum linear program (HiGHS).

front: Optimisation constraints?
back: ≤ 15% per species; size class by sidewalk width; Shannon diversity floor; no invasive or pest-host species; crown clearance from façades.

front: Which LiDAR, and why is its date useful?
back: ICGC LiDAR flown 26 Sept 2021, leaf-on, ≥ 8 pts/m², CC BY 4.0: gives tree height, crown, LAI proxy, buildings and DTM.

front: What does topo.py do?
back: Priority-Flood flow routing on the DTM + buildings: water convergence and flow distance to flood hotspots.

front: What does heat.py compute?
back: Sun position, building shadows, elliptical shadows of ellipsoid crowns with opacity from LAI and leaf month; summer shade = benefit, winter shade = cost.

front: What does season.py add?
back: A leaf-on calendar per species and storm months, so runoff is an expected value over the storm season.

front: Rule for every parameter in tool code?
back: It is either sourced (cited) or marked ASSUMPTION.

front: Name three ASSUMPTION parameters in the tool.
back: CAPTURE_M = 100 m (flow path to hotspot), OP_BARE = 0.35 (leafless crown opacity), R_OFF = 0.5 (leaf-off LAI ratio).

front: What are the two front-ends of the tool?
back: Grasshopper (primary, computational designer, with Ladybug) and a later web app for non-technical users using the fast heat proxy.

front: How are species without measurements handled?
back: Genus or leaf-habit class values with a range; every result re-run at the low and high end (sensitivity).

front: How much do Porta's current street trees cut runoff (T2-60)?
back: 1.85% of total runoff (2.9% on open space); range 0.4–4.0% across s and T.

front: What happens to runoff during the transition to young trees?
back: Any young replacement ≈ +0.7% runoff ≈ 37% (more than a third) of the current street-tree benefit lost.

front: What did Cortinovis et al. 2022 find for Barcelona?
back: 20,170 new street trees raised runoff retention only from 50.18% to 50.76% for a 20 mm event (city-wide, trees as land cover).

front: Optimised vs random palette, summer shade (tool v0)?
back: +16% summer shade, robust across 8 sensitivity variants (15 Oct re-run; was +14%). But about 5% more winter shade than the random palette.

front: What is the no-regret swap?
back: Summer-only → balanced layout: ~90 Tipuana swapped for Jacaranda, same summer shade, only 2% less winter shade (15 Oct re-run with Jacaranda mostly in leaf in January). Not robust: it vanishes in 3 of 8 variants. Superseded (old calendar): −9%.

front: How does placement follow the buildings?
back: Partly: the winter-bare Melia gets the sunniest winter positions (87% of winter hours in sun), evergreen Brachychiton far less (29%); but the winter-bare Styphnolobium (34%) and Pyrus (26%) also sit in winter-shaded streets.

front: Did any replacement layout reach S0?
back: No: mature planes still give more shade than any replacement layout.

front: Open problem found in tool v0?
back: Whether hotspot runoff follows the runoff weight: it did not on 8 Oct, it mostly does on 15 Oct (Spearman −0.73), and it varies only 0.5% across weights, so the per-position water potential is still unverified.

front: Name four limits to state openly.
back: Flood index not depth (RESCCUE depth now public, routing not a flood map); LiDAR LAI proxy probably low; same s for all species; volume only (no sewer or ponding); H3 true by construction; runoff part of H1 may be not resolved.

front: Which TRL and innovation type should you claim?
back: TRL 3 (experimental proof of concept on Porta); process innovation delivered as a tool.

front: What is missing according to the seminar checklist?
back: Stakeholder validation (interviews, user walkthrough), an actor map, and naming innovation type and TRL.

front: Answer: 'Is a 2% effect worth a thesis?'
back: The thesis is the method and the trade-off, not a big runoff number; H3 states the limit openly, and the heat side may dominate.

front: Answer: 'What if the scope is too narrow?'
back: Widen the tree into a system: add the tree pit as one design variable; soil as 2–3 literature options; carbon reported, not optimised.

front: Which species was added as the seventh candidate, when and why?
back: Styphnolobium japonicum (formerly Sophora japonica), by user decision on 14 Oct; named in the press; only 5 trees in Porta.

front: Where do Styphnolobium's crown and LAI come from, and what are they?
back: A LiDAR sample from one 1 km tile outside Porta: 367 trees on 25 streets without possibly merged crowns give crown 5.32 m, LAI 2.12 (all 607 trees: 6.43 m / 2.28).

front: How does Styphnolobium rank for runoff (15 Oct)?
back: 5th of 8 palettes (aggregate), 4th of 7 (grid); replacing planes with it adds runoff (+92.5 m³, +0.52% at T2-60). The earlier 'first place' used only 5 Porta trees and is superseded.

front: What is Δmin for the runoff part of H1?
back: 91 m³: 0.9 mm of interception over the street crown area, 0.5% of T2-60 runoff; fixed before the runs. Stricter bar: 187 m³.

front: What does 'not resolved by the model' mean for H1?
back: If the best layout beats S1 by less than Δmin, the runoff part of H1 is neither supported nor rejected. Accepted as a valid outcome (user, provisional, 14 Oct). Today: 78 m³ (worst case 38.5) → not resolved.

front: Why is the falling % benefit with return period not a real test?
back: With the v1 LAI proxy every crown is full at every design storm, so I = min(P, S) makes the intercepted volume constant and the percentage falls purely because the denominator grows. That is arithmetic, not evidence - which is why H3 was withdrawn on 19 Oct.

front: What does Dong et al. 2026 do, and what does it lack?
back: NSGA-III over species mixes for stormwater and microclimate (+ air quality, carbon) in Philadelphia; heat = building-energy proxy, runoff = i-Tree Eco, no tree positions (species shares per 0.25 km² cell).

front: Name the three candidate contribution statements.
back: A. Method: species + positions vs UTCI and runoff, LiDAR crowns, trait table, leaf-on interception. B. Knowledge: cooling vs interception trade-off for the city palette in Porta. C. (optional) Validation of the heat proxy against Ladybug.

front: Why does 'share of points > 32 °C' fail on the hottest day?
back: On the hottest El Prat day even full shade is ≥ 32 °C in 5 of 6 afternoon hours, so sun and shade count alike: the metric saturates.

front: How big is the sun–shade UTCI gap, and how big is model error?
back: 2.3–4.7 °C (full shade, a lower bound for a tree) vs Ladybug error of about 1–2 °C; so trust layout rankings more than absolute values.

front: What is the heat metric, and why not the peak hour?
back: DECIDED 19 Oct: mean UTCI over 12-17 h on the DDY cooling design day, with the hottest real day as a check. The peak hour saturates - on the hottest El Prat day even full shade is >= 32 C in 5 of 6 afternoon hours - so no layout could show a benefit.

front: Recommended weather forcing (pending)?
back: El Prat TMYx 2011–2025 EPW and DDY, file wind, no offset; sensitivities: city station file, city-terrain wind, +1.5 °C urban offset.

front: What did the routing vs RESCCUE check show?
back: ROC AUC 0.52 overall, but the top 0.5% of open ground by upstream area is wet in 58–80% of cases (1.7–2.6× random): routing finds convergence points, not a flood map; hotspots stay tied to the atlas index.

front: Are the RESCCUE flood-depth maps available?
back: Yes: T10 and T100 (present/future) as public CARTO tables of the Resilience Atlas, found 13 Oct; licence email sent to Barcelona Regional the same day.

front: Why does Ladybug's missing transpiration matter less in Porta?
back: Transpiration per leaf area is lowest in Mediterranean climates and ~10× lower for trees in paved pits than over grass, while shade cools asphalt the most (Rahman et al. 2019).

front: What did the iNaturalist photo check show about winter leaf state?
back: 170 Barcelona photos, Dec–Mar: Tipuana 100% in leaf in Jan (base case holds), drops leaves Feb–Mar; Jacaranda 79% in leaf in Jan, none bare before March, contrary to the old calendar (bare Jan–Mar). New calendar adopted 15 Oct.

front: Did the summer–winter trade-off survive the photo-based leaf calendar (15 Oct)?
back: Yes: winter-heavy vs balanced gives −20% winter shade for −18% summer shade, robust in all 8 variants (winter −14 to −23%, summer −17 to −20%). It now uses the winter-bare Pyrus and Styphnolobium instead of Tipuana.

front: In one line: what transfers and what does not?
back: The code is site-agnostic by construction, the evidence is not. The routing, sun and crown-shadow geometry and SCS-CN kernels carry no local constant; traits, leaf calendar, storm season, flood map and the 15% cap are all local.

front: Which module files are local by construction?
back: heat.py (Barcelona design days and hours), runoff.py (calibrated runoff_params.json + the PDISBA IDF loaded at import), site.py, season.py, layout.py. As a file, only topo.py is constant-free.

front: What are the four degrees of transfer T0–T3?
back: T0 another Barcelona neighbourhood (Sant Antoni, days, same data); T1 another open-data Mediterranean city (Florence, new adapter + 6 datasets, 2–3 weeks); T2 a city missing the point cloud or the inventory (Bologna has ~87,000 trees and a 2023 leaf-on classified survey, but no LAS is served); T3 another climate — out of scope and not claimed. All costs are order-of-magnitude estimates, not measured.

front: Name the three inputs that do not travel (worst first).
back: CLOUD · MAP · TRAITS: (1) a classified leaf-on point cloud (the LAI proxy, so both objectives); (2) a city pluvial flood map (our routing is not one, AUC 0.52); (3) traits and phenology, which get worse on transfer.

front: Why does a 1 m DSM not replace a point cloud?
back: A DSM gives height and crown width but no gap fraction, and LAI = −ln(gap fraction)/k. Without it, species differences collapse to crown size and the measured LAI is replaced by database values.

front: How much worse does the trait gap get on transfer?
back: A species-level runoff or heat value exists for 40% of trees in Barcelona and 19% in Florence (7% with both).

front: What does Florence have, and what is missing?
back: ~82,000 public trees, a 1 km IDF grid (LSPP 2012) and a published pluvial index (Pacetti's PFI) — but the IDF grid's shortest fitted duration is 1 h (so 10–60 min storms are an extrapolation), the PFI is a relative 1–42 rank with no depth or return period under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and terrain is only 1 m DTM/DSM rasters: the point cloud is request-only, and the request is drafted but not yet sent.

front: Why can't Florence's Life Escapos LAI column replace the point cloud?
back: Its lai values are synthetic: a deterministic function of species and DBH (51 of 68 species flat, the other 17 an exact DBH power law, log–log R² = 1.0000). Tested 18 Oct. Licence CC BY-NC 4.0.

front: Why is Mataró the Catalan fallback (19 Oct)?
back: Of the two finalists checked, it is the only one with a published design storm of its own (PDCLAM 2003, 5–120 min) — though those sub-hourly values are themselves a Témez extrapolation, i.e. availability, not independent measurement. It also has the same ICGC leaf-on classified product (flown 20 July 2021, not Porta's 26 Sept mission), the same climate zone and the same CRS (EPSG:25831), so the leaf calendar and storm season stay inside their anchors — but still have to be re-derived.

front: How is Mataró's tree data split?
back: 17,204 street trees by composition (2016 master plan; the "117 species" are table rows including cultivars, 108 distinct binomials), and 79,748 positions in the municipal GeoPackage with no species, no DBH and no height. Without the joined per-tree table, species must be assigned probabilistically from the composition, which turns a species-level transfer test into a composition-weighted one. Licence UNKNOWN for every Mataró asset.

front: What is the species overlap with Porta, and what is the catch?
back: Mataró 52.2% of its top-30 species counting only species with ≥5 Porta trees (about 46% of its whole street stock), 92.9% at genus; Florence 43.5% of its top-30 (about a third of its inventory), 74.0% at genus. Not like-for-like: Mataró and Porta are street-tree inventories, Florence's counts park trees too; the Mataró shares are the 2016 vintage.

front: Why not Badalona?
back: It shares Porta's LiDAR mission day (26 Sept 2021 — a convenience, not a validity condition) and has the better gauge record, but no open tree inventory was found and it has no design rainfall of its own: the only route is to borrow Barcelona's IDF, which makes the transfer test circular.

front: What did the 22-city Catalan LiDAR screening find?
back: Dates read from the per-point GPS time: 18 cities leaf-on and classified, 2 leaf-on but unclassified (Girona, Vic), 1 only partly leaf-on and unclassified (Figueres, April), 1 leaf-off (Manresa, November). Caveat: one 150 × 150 m clip per city centre, not municipality-wide.

front: What is the strongest negative result of the Catalan screening?
back: No Catalan city publishes a city-wide pluvial hazard or depth map: the ACA lists 44 pluvial municipalities but the ARPSI polygon is the municipal boundary, and the one exception (Vila-seca i Salou) is an 8.54 km² ARPSI. Barcelona's RESCCUE depth model is the only city-wide pluvial depth model found in Catalonia — which is why Porta was the right calibration site.

front: Mataró's design storm looks 19–32% drier than Barcelona's. What do you answer?
back: Most of it is method, not climate: Barcelona's PDISBA value is an across-gauge envelope (+24% over the gauge mean), Mataró's a central Gumbel estimate with an analytic sub-daily shape. Harmonised, 66% of the gap goes at 10 min and 77–80% at 20–60 min, leaving 0.93 at T = 10 and 1.00 at T = 2. Residuals to state: the daily legs still use different frequency laws (Gumbel vs SQRT-ET max), and the transfer city's sub-hourly curve is an assumption.

front: Why is the flat harmonised ratio not a finding?
back: It is an identity: both cities sit in the I1/Id = 11 region, so the Témez duration factor cancels at both ends, and any two such cities would give a flat line. The evidence is the raw ratio reversing direction with duration, which climate cannot do.

front: Which design storm is published for no candidate transfer city?
back: T = 1 yr. Barcelona's PDISBA has one, which is the problem; PDCLAM's "T = 1" column is the Gumbel T = 1.001 limit and must not be used.

front: How does the research question itself have to change on transfer?
back: It is a Barcelona decision (15% cap, planes ~29%, a named palette). Outside Barcelona only L'Hospitalet has a formally approved 15% cap, and Mataró has none, so the decision variable becomes species at renewal positions or at new plantable cells, with a diversity constraint and the city's own suitability list instead of a named palette. The optimiser does not change; the framing does.

front: Which parameters must be re-derived, not copied?
back: s = 1.75 mm/LAI (already a transfer from Freiburg), the storm months (78% May–Oct), the leaf calendar and R_OFF, the heat design days, HAZARD_HIGH = 40 (a Barcelona-specific index) and CAPTURE_M = 100 m. OP_BARE and k travel, but as assumptions.

front: What proves the routing is not a flood map?
back: Against RESCCUE depth it gives ROC AUC 0.52; only the tail informs — the top 0.5% of open ground by upstream area is wet in 58–80% of cases, 1.7–2.6× random. So hotspots must come from a municipal map.

front: Hasn't the city already solved the replacement problem?
back: No. The master plan fixes how much of each species (15% cap; planes to 12%) and the 2011 guide which tree size fits which sidewalk. The per-position choice comes from criteria the city has not published, and nothing the city publishes measures heat or runoff.

front: Why does the master plan cap species at 15%, and where does the number come from?
back: Pest and disease risk of a monoculture, climate resilience, biodiversity. No document derives 15; it is looser than Santamour's 10% and is the regional convention.

front: Over what does the 15% cap apply?
back: City-wide, over the urban fabric (~201,600 municipal trees in 2017, including squares). Never per neighbourhood, so the tool's Porta-local cap is an ASSUMPTION.

front: How does sidewalk width set the tree size (2011 guide)?
back: < 2.5 m no tree; < 3.5 m small (crown < 4 m, spacing 7 m); 3.5–6 m medium (crown 4–6 m, 9 m); > 6 m large (crown > 6 m, 13 m).

front: Which two master-plan targets can conflict at one position?
back: No species above 15% (moving away from planes serves it, though Celtis is already close) and tree cover up to 30% of the urban surface (a small-crowned replacement works against it).

front: Crown area of the replacements vs a plane, at equal trunk size (Porta, 2nd and 3rd trunk classes)?
back: Tipuana and Jacaranda 89–107%, Melia 71–81%, Celtis 32–52%, Pyrus 35%, Brachychiton 24–27%. Raw medians mislead because the species differ in trunk-class mix.

front: What is S1 since v6?
back: The city's own replacement: the 2026 target mix (press) assigned at random within the 2011 sizing rule, over several seeds. Replaced by the city's internal list if obtained.
